summary:
Chocó is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework of Colombia, whose formal legal order is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official who defended the change described those examinations as profoundly invasive of privacy rights and rooted in unacceptable prejudice. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried 'trans' and 'non-binary' markers since November 2025.

The substantive rights attached to that framework are settled. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, same-sex marriage has been available since April 2016, when the Constitutional Court legalised it and Colombia became the fourth country in the region to do so, and same-sex couples have held joint adoption rights since 2015. A national LGBTI policy text covers rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and states that national entities may not refuse to recognise same-sex couples.

The framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a video showed Sara Millerey, 32, drowning in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands; her mother Sandra Borja said they killed her for being who she was, President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024, and more than 40 were killed in 2023. Reporting of 6 August 2025 found that the killings continued at the hands of armed gangs after the Millerey case, framing being queer in parts of the country as signing your own death sentence.

Some of that targeting is organised by armed actors. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024. In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announced a 'social cleansing' naming faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes as legitimate military targets; a trans woman standing as a local election candidate was given one week by three armed men to leave town, hid for a week and then fled at night, and a second trans woman said a friend had been killed. Trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men. Discrimination narrows trans women in the department mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

In Chocó the operating reality is that armed groups rather than the departmental police regulate conduct, and trans women are displaced from departments such as Chocó. The Caquetá campaign, where flyers circulated on the streets and through WhatsApp and trans women were ordered out of town, is the closest documented model for the territorial violence and displacement inflicted on Chocó by armed actors; the departmental source itself produced no specific finding.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity, and the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
tangentialFactors:
Chocó's legal position is indistinguishable from Colombia's national one; what distinguishes it is who enforces. Departments such as Caquetá and Guajira show the pattern that governs Chocó's territory: armed groups distributing kill lists and 'social cleansing' notices, naming trans people explicitly, and issuing deadlines for individuals to leave town. Caquetá is used here as a comparator, not as evidence about Chocó itself.

Displacement is the main channel through which the national framework fails trans people in Chocó. Reporting records trans women being pushed out of departments including Chocó, and the national policy text covering protection as victims of armed conflict is the element of Colombian law that speaks directly to that experience.

The gap between formal protection and lived outcome has been stated at the highest level. The UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission praised the reforms while describing a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily experience, and killing figures continued to rise through 2024 and 2025 despite marriage equality, joint adoption, notary-based marker change and anti-discrimination law.

Economic exclusion compounds the physical risk. Where discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, sex work places them in contact with the same armed actors running the flyer campaigns, which helps explain why displacement rather than complaint is the usual response to a death threat.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on national identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since the June 2015 rule change, and self-recognition has been sufficient since 1993 with no surgical requirement. Identification cards have carried 'trans' and 'non-binary' markers since November 2025.

The 2011 anti-discrimination law, marriage equality since April 2016 and joint adoption since 2015 apply nationwide, and national entities may not refuse to recognise same-sex couples.

Residents are covered by the 2016 Ministry of Interior decree, which sets procedural obligations for government institutions in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and by the May 2018 executive decree extending guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

People targeted in the conflict have a specific avenue: in July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging gender persecution as a crime against humanity, and the UN Human Rights Committee registered concern.

In practice, trans residents face an employment ceiling that confines most to hairdressing or sex work, and they are displaced from departments including Chocó by armed groups that regulate conduct in place of the departmental police. No Chocó enforcement record under the anti-discrimination law or the 2016 decree is documented in these sources.
